BALANCE INNOVATION - SAMPLE CLIENT SCREEN-FREE AUDIO FOR KIDS WORKING BRIEF
v0.14 - 19 NOV 2026
01 - Summary

What we learned

Executive summary

Parents want a player they can hand to a young child so that the child listens and no screen is involved. The listening goes well. The trouble comes before it, in setup and content cost, and after it, in wear.

131
parent and reviewer comments read, each with a source link
From parent forums, retailer reviews and press reviews. A sample, not a count of all owners.
0.93
pain share while keeping the player working
The highest of any stage. 15 comments, about batteries that stop charging, broken buttons and lost cards.
0.09
pain share while the child is listening
The lowest of any stage except Modify. 33 comments, many about bedtime.
0.70
pain share at setup
10 comments. Several describe needing a phone, an app or Wi-Fi to load a player sold as screen-free.
THE ASK
A fictional maker of children's products asked where a screen-free audio player for ages 1 to 8 could do better than what parents already use.
The client is made up for this sample brief. Everything else is real public evidence, collected on 19 Nov 2026.
WHAT WE LOOKED AT
Four kinds of player: card players, figure players, preloaded and library-lent players, and the workarounds (CD, MP3, an old phone).
Yoto and Tonies carry most of the comments because they carry most of the sales. Playaway, library lending and CD players give the contrast.
HOW TO READ IT
Pain share is the share of comments that are negative, counting a mixed comment as half.
It shows where parents struggle. It is not a failure rate. Quotes link to the comments behind them.
Five findingsEach finding is a full sentence tied to the comments behind it. Press Show sources at the top right to see the comment numbers. The Territories tab turns the findings into five places to work.
  • The listening is the part that works. Bedtime comments are the happiest in the set: a child falls asleep to it, or a three-hour settle shrinks (E0016, E0024, E0044, E0058). Of the 13 comments coded to bedtime and sleep, 10 are positive and none is negative.
  • The trouble starts at setup, and a phone is often in it. Parents who bought a screen-free player describe feeding it from a screen, or finding it needs an app and Wi-Fi to play new cards (E0001, E0004, E0037, E0067, E0072).
  • Content cost is the most commented theme. 20 of the 131 comments are coded to it. Parents compare the price of a story card or figure with the minutes it holds, and some quote the numbers (E0049, E0078, E0027). Workarounds are common: blank figures, make-your-own cards, free library audio (E0020, E0051, E0102).
  • Players break in ways a toddler causes. Dropped units lose a button, mounts snap, batteries stop charging and loose cards go missing (E0006, E0022, E0046, E0062, E0073). Some owners report the opposite and call it sturdy (E0019, E0028, E0075).
  • Age fit splits the field. Parents of Yoto players report use at 8, 9 and 10 (E0003, E0079, E0091). Parents of Tonies players split between 'outgrown by 3' and 'still used daily after two years' (E0052, E0081). Parents of older children say the choice for 7 and up is thin (E0005, E0053).
What this means for a makerFour actions, each with the reason, written so the room can pick one.
  • Make the first week work with no phone, because the people who chose screen-free are the people least happy to be handed a screen (E0037, E0067).
  • Show the minutes and the price per hour on every pack, because parents are already doing that sum in public (E0049, E0078).
  • Design controls for a two-year-old's hand first, because tap-to-skip and small dials are where toddlers get stuck (E0030, E0061, E0076), and one parent says the same player works for a child from about 2 (E0094).
  • Give a dropped, chewed or lost-card player a plan, because owners judge the product on how it survives the first year (E0019, E0028, E0084).
Where to start on the six concept cardsA first pass at order, by effort, and by how many parent comments speak directly to the need. Direct means the comment is about that exact problem. This is a judgment from a small sample, to be argued with.

02 - Concept Cards

Concept cards

Here are six ideas for Sample Client, a fictional maker of children's products, to improve screen-free audio players for children aged 1 to 8. Three are about content and selling, and three are about the player and its cards. Each card shows the parent comments behind the idea, the closest product on sale, and the main question to answer next. The sketches are rough drawings to start a conversation. No idea has been built, tested with children or costed. Product safety for young children (small parts, batteries, volume limits), content licensing and library handling are not assessed here and each would need checking before any idea moves ahead.

Minutes and Price Per Hour Label

Tier 1 - Content and sellingContent and selling
The Opportunity

Parents already do this sum in public. One writes that they refuse to spend $9 for something 20 minutes long, and another says the price is a bit much for a figure with 20 minutes of content. A label that does the sum first lets the parent compare a 20 minute card with a three hour pack at the shelf.

Solution

Every card or figure pack carries a panel on the front with three lines: the number of minutes, the price, and the price per hour. These are illustrative packs, not products on sale. A pack of 20 minutes at $9.00 reads $27.00 per hour. A pack of three hours ten minutes at $19.00 reads $6.00 per hour. The same panel goes on the web listing. Nothing in the player changes.

The Sketch
Fits

Any card, figure or disc pack Sample Client sells.

Benchmark

No product page read for this brief states price per hour. Yoto Mini ships with one free make-your-own card and Tonies figures list near $19.99, so parents have both a free and a costly point to compare against.

Price position - estimate

Cost drivers: label print only, no new tooling. Not estimated, and no client cost data exists for this sample.

Must-haves
  • Three lines on the front. Minutes, price, and price per hour, in that order.
  • One rule for the sum. Price divided by minutes, times sixty, rounded to the cent.
  • Same panel online. The listing shows the same three lines above the fold.
Why It’s New

We searched the product pages listed on the Context tab and found no pack that states price per hour. We did not search shelf packaging in stores, so a store may already do this.

The Evidence3 confirmed - 1 inferred
CONFIRMEDA parent says they refuse to spend $9 for something that is 20 minutes long. E0078 Ask MetaFilter, 31 Mar 2024 - Source
CONFIRMEDA parent says the price is a bit much for figures with only 20 minutes of content. E0049 Trustpilot, Nov 2026
CONFIRMEDYoto Mini ships with one free make-your-own card, and pre-made story cards are sold separately. Target listing - Source
INFERREDShowing price per hour will make long packs look better value than short ones, which may move sales toward longer content. We have not tested this. Our reading
Feasibility NoteMain question: Will the label raise sales of long packs, or make short packs look poor and hurt them?
A label is a print change. The open questions are commercial. Short cards may look expensive beside long ones, and content partners may not want a price per hour printed next to their title. A shelf test with two label versions would answer the first question. A conversation with two content partners would answer the second.
What’s Next3 steps
  • Mock up the panel on three illustrative packs: $9.00 for 20 minutes, $19.00 for 3 hours 10 minutes and one free card.
  • Show the mock-ups to ten parents and ask which pack they would pick and why.
  • Ask two content partners how they would feel about the line.

Listening Post at the Shelf

Tier 1 - Content and sellingContent and selling
The Opportunity

One parent says a card gives only a very limited preview of what it contains. Another calls the player an expensive automated reader. A parent who can hear the product, and hear a child-friendly sample, answers both before paying.

Solution

A shelf unit holds sample cards beside a dock with the same speaker as the player. A parent taps a sample card on the dock and hears thirty seconds of that story. A second panel names the minutes and the price per hour. The unit also carries a demo player on a tether, so the parent can see the controls a two-year-old would use.

The Sketch
Fits

Sample Client shelf space and the retail partners that stock it.

Benchmark

Toy shops often tether a demo unit, and the leading brands may already run try-me displays. We have not checked store displays.

Price position - estimate

Cost drivers: a shelf fixture, a small speaker, sample cards and restocking. Not estimated.

Must-haves
  • Sample cards on the shelf. Sample cards play thirty seconds of real content.
  • Same speaker as the player. So the parent hears the real sound.
  • Tethered demo player. So a parent can try the controls.
Why It’s New

Not checked. Try-me displays may already exist, so a store visit comes before any claim that this is new. The sample audio would also need content rights.

The Evidence2 confirmed - 1 inferred
CONFIRMEDA parent says the card provides only a very limited preview of what it contains. E0012 Trustpilot UK, 19 Sep 2026
CONFIRMEDA parent calls it an expensive automated version of someone reading a book to him. E0054 Mumsnet, 20 Sep 2022
INFERREDA listening post may lift trial in shops, but we have no sales data on this. Our reading
Feasibility NoteMain question: Will retailers give up shelf space for a unit that plays audio, which can be loud in a shop?
A shelf unit is injection molding and a small speaker, and tethered demos are standard in toy retail. The open questions are noise in a shop, cleaning and who restocks the sample cards. A pilot in two stores would answer them.
What’s Next3 steps
  • Draw the fixture to the width of a standard toy shelf bay.
  • Ask two retail buyers how they handle sound in the toy aisle.
  • Run a two-store pilot with a volume limit and a headphone option.

Library Lending Kit

Tier 4 - New vendor or technologyNew vendor or technology
The Opportunity

Libraries already lend audio. One parent says Libby audiobooks are free with a library card, and another says waits can take forever. Older comments say library catalogs of children's Playaway titles were small. A kit lent with the player removes the setup step and the screen.

Solution

A library lends a bag with a player and a themed set of six to ten cards, such as bedtime, car trips or first words. The card set is preloaded, so no app, phone or Wi-Fi is involved. After 21 days the family returns the kit, or buys the set at a stated price. The library gets a returns report so it knows what was borrowed.

The Sketch
Fits

A lending model that libraries already run for audiobooks. The new part is a reusable player with themed card sets and a buy-the-set exit.

Benchmark

Playaway audiobook players are lent by libraries, such as Greenville County Library, which lends them for 21 days at four per card with no fee listed. Playaway Launchpad is a preloaded children's tablet that libraries lend.

Price position - estimate

Cost drivers: a ruggedized bag, a multi-card set, cataloging and loss replacement. Not estimated.

Must-haves
  • Player and themed card set in one bag. Lent as one item.
  • Preloaded content. No app, phone or Wi-Fi needed.
  • Return or buy. Families can keep the set.
Why It’s New

Playaway already lends preloaded players through libraries, and the Launchpad is aimed at children. What may be new is a card format lent with a reusable player, and the buy-the-set exit. We did not search patents beyond three.

The Evidence4 confirmed
CONFIRMEDA parent says Libby audiobooks are free as long as you have a library card. E0102 Mumsnet, 20 Aug 2025
CONFIRMEDA parent says it sometimes takes forever to get a book from the library. E0123 The Well-Trained Mind forums, 2019
CONFIRMEDGreenville County Library lends Playaway players for 21 days, four per card, with no fee listed. Greenville County Library - Source
CONFIRMEDUS libraries lend preloaded Playaway Launchpad tablets that need no Wi-Fi or downloads. Central Rappahannock Regional Library - Source
Feasibility NoteMain question: Will libraries buy a kit that needs sanitizing and returns tracking, and will families buy the set after borrowing?
Libraries lend preloaded players today, but a kit of loose cards adds problems libraries dislike: missing pieces, cataloging, cleaning and replacement cost. Most libraries also do not sell collection items back to patrons, so the buy-the-set exit may not work. Lending terms for audio aimed at children differ from consumer terms. Interviews with three librarians who run collections for children and a content partner come before anything else.
What’s Next3 steps
  • Interview three children's librarians about loan length, damage and cleaning.
  • Ask a content partner what a lending license would cost.
  • Sketch the bag and the returns label.

Push Bar Skip

Tier 2 - Change an existing productChange an existing product
The Opportunity

Parents of two-year-olds say tap to skip is too hard for them, that dials may be advanced for younger toddlers, and that hitting the box to move tracks is infuriating. Another says the whole point is that kids can use it completely independently from 2 or so.

Solution

The top of the player carries a wide push bar. A press anywhere on it skips to the next track. A long press replays the last one. The card slot and a big stop button stay where they are. The bar is about the width of the player so a fist, a palm or an elbow works.

The Sketch
Fits

The next version of a card player in Sample Client's range.

Benchmark

Yoto Player and Toniebox 2 are the two reference players. Parents describe dials on one and tap-to-skip on the other as sticking points.

Price position - estimate

Cost drivers: a wider cap and switch, a stronger spring. Small against the player cost, but not estimated.

Must-haves
  • Bar across the full width. Any part of a hand can press it.
  • Press skips, long press replays. Two actions, one control.
  • Stop button stays. A separate, large stop, fixed so it cannot detach.
Why It’s New

A wide skip bar is a small change on a player. We read two products and did not survey every player, so one may already have it.

The Evidence3 confirmed - 1 inferred
CONFIRMEDA parent says tap to skip was really hard to use and left the player unusable by their 2 year old. E0061 Target review, Dec 2025
CONFIRMEDA reviewer for The Bump notes the dials might be advanced for younger toddlers. E0030 The Bump
CONFIRMEDA parent says the whole point is that kids can use it completely independently from 2 or so. E0094 Mumsnet
INFERREDA single wide bar is likely easier than a button or dial for a small hand, but we have not tested it with children. Our reading
Feasibility NoteMain question: Will a bar that is easy to press also get pressed by accident in a bag or a bed?
A bar is a cap over a tactile switch, a familiar mechanism. The open questions are accidental presses, which a lock or a firmer spring would address, and the force a two-year-old can apply. A bench test with a force gauge and a session with small children would settle it.
What’s Next3 steps
  • Print three bar prototypes at different widths and spring forces.
  • Test with six children aged 2 to 4 under adult supervision, with parental consent.
  • Measure the force needed and set a spring target.

Card Dock and Bumper

Tier 2 - Change an existing productChange an existing product
The Opportunity

Parents say loose cards are easy to lose, that a card player does not come with a way to store its cards, and that a dropped player lost a side button. A parent also says a child broke the mount of a player. Others say cards and shells are sturdy, so the idea is to keep what is sturdy and fix what is lost or broken.

Solution

The lid of the player holds five cards in a shallow tray. A soft rubber bumper wraps the four corners. A parent can take the player and a handful of cards in one hand without a separate pouch. The bumper is replaceable if it wears.

The Sketch
Fits

The next version of a card player in Sample Client's range.

Benchmark

Yoto sells cards separately and parents report losing them. Third-party silicone cases and card holders exist for card players, and we have not catalogued them.

Price position - estimate

Cost drivers: one extra mold for the lid tray and an overmolded or slip-on bumper. Not estimated.

Must-haves
  • Card tray in the lid. Holds about five cards.
  • Soft corner bumper. Takes drops on the corners.
  • Replaceable bumper. A worn bumper can be swapped.
Why It’s New

Third-party cases and holders exist, so the novelty is building them into the player. We have not searched patents beyond three.

The Evidence4 confirmed
CONFIRMEDA parent says it is easy to lose the cards as they come loose. E0022 Mumsnet, 11 Sep 2020
CONFIRMEDA Reviewed.com staff reviewer says the player does not come with a way to store the content cards. E0041 Reviewed
CONFIRMEDA parent says the player fell a couple of times and the left side button was affected. E0006 Trustpilot, 2026
CONFIRMEDA parent says the cards are as sturdy as a debit card and pretty indestructible. E0019 Mumsnet
Feasibility NoteMain question: Will a lid that holds cards stay closed in a bag, and will the extra tooling raise unit cost too much?
A tray in a lid and an overmolded bumper are standard plastics and rubber processes, and the cost is mainly an extra mold. The player range starts at age 1, so loose cards and a replaceable bumper raise small-part and choking questions that must be checked against product safety rules for young children before going further. A drop test from table height onto a hard floor and a bag-carry test would show whether it survives and stays shut.
What’s Next3 steps
  • Model the lid tray in CAD and print one at full size.
  • Cost an overmolded bumper against a slip-on silicone sleeve.
  • Run a one metre drop test on three bumper designs.

Self-Playing Card

Tier 3 - New product, existing vendorNew product, existing vendor
The Opportunity

Parents who chose a screen-free player describe needing Wi-Fi to play a physical card, and spending evenings on a screen feeding it. One says the card should come premade so it plays without connecting to Wi-Fi first.

Solution

The card holds its audio in a small flash chip behind a contact strip. The player reads the strip when the card slides in. Content plays at once, with no download, no app and no Wi-Fi. A card can still be updated through the app for parents who want that, but they do not need to.

The Sketch
Fits

A new card format for the next player, using a supplier Sample Client already uses for printing and electronics.

Benchmark

Playaway devices come with the audiobook preloaded and need no internet. Yoto and Tonies need a connection to load new cards, and the Yoto Mini then plays offline.

Price position - estimate

Cost drivers: a flash chip and contact strip on every card, which is the main open number. Not estimated.

Must-haves
  • Audio stored on the card. No download is needed.
  • Contact strip. Reads when the card slides in.
  • Plays offline. No app or Wi-Fi at first use.
Why It’s New

Preloaded audio is not new, as Playaway shows. What may be new is a swappable flash card in a card-player format. We did not search for products or patents beyond the three read.

The Evidence3 confirmed - 1 inferred
CONFIRMEDA parent says the card should come premade to work in the player so it can play without connecting to Wi-Fi beforehand. E0004 Trustpilot, Sep 2026
CONFIRMEDA parent says they needed the player connected to Wi-Fi to play the physical cards, which they did not understand when buying. E0011 Trustpilot Canada, Oct 2026
CONFIRMEDA blogger writes that Playaway books are pre-downloaded, so there is no worry about the internet. E0129 Imagination Soup, 2022
INFERREDA card with its own chip costs more than a printed card, and we do not know by how much. Our reading
Feasibility NoteMain question: What does a card with a flash chip add to unit cost, and will parents pay for it?
Small flash memory and a contact strip are common electronics. The open questions are cost at card volumes, contact life through hundreds of insertions, and three harder ones: audio on a swappable card is easy to copy, so content owners may demand encryption or usage reporting; exposed contacts and a chip are a small-part question for young children; and an app update path would bring back the app the card is meant to remove. A quote from two chip suppliers and a durability test of the contacts would answer it.
What’s Next4 steps
  • Ask two content partners what copy protection they would require.
  • Ask two flash suppliers for a quote at 10,000 and 100,000 cards.
  • Build ten sample cards with a contact strip and run a 500 insertion test.
  • Interview eight parents about a price premium for a card that plays offline.

03 - Territories

Opportunity territories

Executive summary

Five territories, each anchored on a different part of the job map. We would start with setup and upkeep for business impact, and with age fit for the richest ideation. Bedtime and car listening already work, so the job there is to protect them.

25
Setup and upkeep that need no phone, app or Wi-Fi
Pain share 0.84, covering three job map steps. The highest of the five.
23
Content that costs less per hour and can be previewed
Pain share 0.48. Price complaints run through the Confirm stage.
35
A player a two-year-old can run and an eight-year-old still wants
Pain share 0.21. The most comments, mostly positive.
19
Listening routines at bedtime and in the car
Pain share 0.05. The part parents love.
READING THE FIVE
T4, choosing the first player, has 29 comments and pain share 0.31 and is not shown above.
Numbers here group job map steps, so they differ from the stage and theme figures on other tabs. The Method tab explains why.
BUSINESS IMPACT
Setup and upkeep that do not need a phone, an app or Wi-Fi.
It carries the most pain (0.84), and the complaint is sharpest for the group that chose screen-free on purpose (E0037, E0067).
IDEATION RICHNESS
A player a two-year-old can run and an eight-year-old still wants.
Many sketchable mechanisms: controls, shell, card or figure format, content for older children. Manufacturing is familiar plastics, electronics and printing.
FASTEST TO TRY
Content that costs less per hour and can be previewed before buying.
Two of the three Tier 1 ideas change labels, packs and shelves, and need no new tooling.
T1 Content that costs less per hour and can be previewed before buyingParents do the price sum themselves and some of them stop. 23 comments, pain share 0.48.

Problem. A parent sees a card or figure at about $9 to $20, learns it holds around twenty minutes, and decides it is too much (E0049, E0078). Others cannot see what is on a card before buying (E0012).

When it bites. At the shelf or the checkout, and again a month later when the child has heard everything twice.

What a better product does. It states minutes and price per hour on the pack, lets the buyer hear a sample, and makes parent-made content easy, because owners who record their own say it cuts the cost (E0020, E0051, E0055).

The catch. Content partners set prices and Sample Client may not control them. Longer stories mean fewer titles to sell.

Market check. Yoto includes one free make-your-own card with the Mini and streams free radio. Libraries lend audio at no fee listed. No product page read states price per hour.

  • Tier 1: Show minutes and price per hour on every pack (E0049, E0078, E0027)
  • Tier 1: A listening post at the shelf that plays a sample when a card or figure is tapped (E0012)
  • Tier 4: A library lending kit with a player and a borrowed set (E0102, E0123, E0114)
T2 A player a two-year-old can run and an eight-year-old still wantsThe listening works when the child can work the controls. 35 comments, pain share 0.21. Most are positive, which is why this territory is about not losing a win.

Problem. Tap-to-skip, small dials and the need to hit the box to change track stop some toddlers (E0030, E0061, E0076). At the other end, a child outgrows the content or the look of the player (E0036, E0052, E0005).

When it bites. At two to three years, when a child first tries it alone, and at six to seven, when stories run thin.

What a better product does. It lets a child skip, replay and stop with one big gesture, and keeps a path to older content, since parents report use at 8, 9 and 10 for card players (E0003, E0079, E0091).

The catch. A control simple enough for a two-year-old must still look right to an eight-year-old.

Market check. Both leaders offer one control scheme. We read no product that offers a second mode for older children.

  • Tier 2: A squeeze or push bar to skip that works with a whole hand (E0030, E0061, E0076)
  • Tier 3: A growing-up mode that unlocks chapters and radio for older children (E0005, E0053)
T3 Setup and upkeep that do not need a phone, an app or Wi-FiThe people who wanted screen-free are the people most annoyed to need a screen to set it up. 25 comments, pain share 0.84.

Problem. New cards need Wi-Fi first, setup runs through a phone app, and a parent spends an evening on a screen feeding the player (E0004, E0011, E0037, E0067, E0072). Then batteries stop charging, buttons fail after drops, and loose cards go missing (E0006, E0022, E0046, E0062).

When it bites. In the first week, and again around month twenty, when a battery fails.

What a better product does. It plays out of the box, loads content without a phone, and survives a drop. Some owners already call the cards and shells sturdy (E0019, E0028, E0075).

The catch. Cards that carry their own audio cost more to make than cards that point to a download.

Market check. Preloaded players, such as Playaway devices, need no internet (E0129). Card players need Wi-Fi to load new cards (E0004, E0011).

  • Tier 2: A card dock in the lid and a rubber bumper (E0022, E0041, E0093, E0006)
  • Tier 3: A card that carries its own audio, so it plays without a Wi-Fi step (E0004, E0011)
T4 Choosing the first player with confidenceParents compare a tablet, a CD player, a card player and a figure player before they buy. 29 comments, pain share 0.31.

Problem. A parent cannot tell the options apart, thinks a screen-free player is an expensive reader, or falls back on an old phone (E0054, E0085, E0101).

When it bites. Before purchase, usually at a gift moment.

What a better product does. It lets the parent hear the product in a shop, or try it, and says plainly what it does and does not need.

The catch. A shop listening post costs fixtures and shelf space, and works only where the client has shelves.

Market check. We found no retail listening post for these players in the pages read.

  • Tier 1: A listening post at the shelf (E0012, E0054)
T5 Listening routines at bedtime and in the carThe most loved part of the product. 19 comments, pain share 0.05. The job is to protect it.

Problem. There is little to fix. The risk is that a change in another territory breaks the routine, such as a new app step before bedtime.

When it bites. At bedtime, when a child cannot settle, and on long drives.

What a better product does. It keeps the sleep timer, the night-light and the stories that settle a child, and adds nothing that needs a screen.

The catch. Parents who use it every night notice any change.

Market check. Yoto has a sleep radio and a night-light (E0016, E0082).

  • Hold: keep bedtime features as they are while changing setup and controls (E0016, E0024, E0044, E0058)

04 - Context

Context

Executive summary

Screen-free audio for children has become a real category. Two companies report fast growth, and pediatric guidance gives parents a reason to look for it.

MARKET
Tonies reported 2025 revenue of 630 million euros and close to 12 million players sold over ten years.
Yoto reported 2024 revenue of 94.8 million pounds, up 86% on 2023. Both figures come from press reports of company filings.
PARENT REASON
The American Academy of Pediatrics says children under 18 months learn best from real-world interaction.
Its page also says heavy solo screen use can delay language and thinking in ages 0 to 5. Last updated 3 June 2026.
LIMIT
Company figures are as reported, not checked against filings by us.
We read three US patents and no market-size report. See the Method tab.
How big and how fastTwo companies, one in figures and one in cards, report growth well ahead of toys in general. The numbers are as press reported them.
  • Tonies: 630 million euros revenue in 2025, close to 12 million players and 150 million figures sold in ten years (The Star, Malaysia, 25 May 2026).
  • Yoto: 94.8 million pounds in 2024, up 86% from 50.9 million pounds in 2023. Revenue was reported up 43% in 2025, with about 22 billion minutes listened in 2025 (RouteNote Radar citing Music Ally, 5 Oct 2026).
  • New Zealand shows the same shape: Tonies box sales doubled from 2024 to 2025 and Yoto listening hours grew 125% over the year (1News NZ, 5 Nov 2026).
  • Libraries are part of the picture. Libraries in the US lend preloaded Playaway Launchpad tablets for children that need no Wi-Fi or downloads (Central Rappahannock Regional Library).

05 - User Signals

User signals

Executive summary

In this sample, parents choose these players to keep screens away, and the listening mostly delivers. The pain sits in setup, in content cost, and in wear, so those are where a new product can earn its place.

131

Forums (about half) and reviews (about half), US and UK.

18 comments. Second highest.

pain share on bedtime and sleep. Price and content cost, the most commented theme, is 0.53.
13 comments, none negative.
The client's hypotheses, testedFive hypotheses a maker would bring to this category, and what the comments say about each.
HypothesisVerdictEvidence
Parents choose audio players to keep screens awaySupportedParents say it beats TV and ask for a device with no search or games (E0066, E0068, E0089, E0118). Pain on this theme is low (0.2).
Young children can run the player aloneSupported, with a catchParents report use from about 2 (E0014, E0094). Skip controls and small dials stop some toddlers (E0030, E0061, E0076).
Content cost decides the purchasePartlyIt is the most repeated complaint (E0049, E0078, E0069). Parents who are happy say the player was the best money spent (E0002) or cut the cost with their own content (E0020, E0051).
The player stays useful into school ageMixedReports of use at 8, 9 and 10 for card players (E0003, E0079, E0091). Figure players are called outgrown by 3 by some (E0052) and used daily two years on by others (E0081).
Setup is easy and needs no phoneNot supportedParents describe needing an app, Wi-Fi or a phone (E0004, E0037, E0063, E0067). One parent found setup smooth and the instructions good (E0013).

Free and borrowed audioLibraries and old phones are the competition on price. Their weak spots are waiting and, for Libby, the need for a phone or tablet, so it is a price comparison and not a like-for-like one.
How to read this: each column is a step in the job. Sub-steps are what people do at that step. Pain points are what goes wrong, written from the comments. Click one for the quotes, why it matters and the desired outcome. Every pain point is a hypothesis built from secondary research. Sourced means it traces to dated entries in the evidence ledger. Thin evidence means fewer than 5 entries. Border colour: coral is pain share 0.50 or higher, gold 0.30 to 0.49, grey 0.15 to 0.29, green below 0.15.

06 - Competitive

Competitive map

Executive summary

Each way of getting audio to a child gives something up. Cards and figures win on ease, and parents describe their content as costly. Phones and libraries win on cost and give up the screen-free promise or speed of access. We did not compute cost per hour across models.

Where the gaps areGaps are places where the comments describe a need and the products read for this brief do not describe an answer. We have not tested every product, so each is a lead to check.
  • Play without a phone. Parents describe wanting cards to play without a Wi-Fi step first (E0004, E0011). Preloaded players already do this (E0129). We did not compare catalog size against card and figure players.
  • Cost per hour on the pack. Parents quote the cost per twenty minutes themselves (E0049, E0078). We saw no product page that states price per hour.
  • A control a two-year-old can use. Skip and dial controls trip toddlers on both leading models (E0030, E0061, E0076).
  • Two children, one player. One parent bought a second player so two children could listen to different things (E0038).
  • Content for 7 and up. Parents of older children call the choice thin (E0005, E0053).

Brand lanes still openWhat no brand in this set claims in the lines read. Each is a lead, not a verdict.
  • The player that never needs a phone. Yoto and Tonies both lean on an app (E0004, E0067). Playaway devices already claim offline play and no data collection, so the open lane is a card or figure format that plays offline, not offline play itself.
  • The honest price per hour. No brand line read states it.
  • The player that grows with the child. Parents already judge on this (E0003, E0052, E0079).

08 - Method

How we did the research

Executive summary

This brief reads 131 public comments and a set of product and market pages collected on 19 November 2026. It is a sample brief with a fictional client, and the sample is small. Treat counts as patterns to test.

What was readEvery comment is one row in an evidence ledger with its source link, date accessed and the exact words used.
  • 131 comments, one per source link: 63 from forums (mostly Mumsnet) and 68 from reviews (Trustpilot, retailer reviews and press reviews written by parents).
  • Product, price, market and patent facts from retailer pages, company pages, press and Google Patents, listed on the Context tab.
  • Markets: United States and United Kingdom. UK comments show pounds. Dates run from 2008 to November 2026.
How quotes were checkedThe reader must be able to check any quote.
  • Each quote is 14 words or fewer, one per source link, and sits in the ledger with the passage it came from.
  • The build stops if a quote shown in the brief does not match its saved extract word for word.
  • Each quote was copied from a search or page-text extract and saved with its source link. The build confirms the quote matches that saved extract. It does not prove the page still says it. On 19 Nov 2026 a reviewer re-opened 9 of the 131 pages and found the quote in each. Re-open the source link before using any quote outside this document.
  • Reddit, Amazon reviews and several retailer review pages could not be read, so those voices are missing.
How comments were codedPlain rules, so the results can be argued with.
  • Each comment was given a stage and step of the job map by the agent that collected it, from the words in the comment.
  • Each comment got one primary theme from ten, by keyword rules, then corrected by hand on 38 comments where the keywords misled. A comment can touch other themes.
  • Pain share is negative comments plus half of mixed comments, over all comments in the group.
Where the evidence is thinNamed so nobody reads more into it than it holds.
  • No saturation claim. With 131 comments, most source groups are too small to test whether more reading would change the themes.
  • Two questions are thin: whether parents build their own content (3 comments) and how libraries, schools and special needs change the picture (9 comments).
  • The accessibility group is 6 comments. The gift-buyer group is 9. They describe and do not rank.
  • The Echo Dot Kids, Miko, Storypod, WhaZoodle, WonderBuddy and Playaway Launchpad rows have product pages but no parent comments.
  • No librarian, retailer buyer or content licensor was interviewed. Their constraints (cataloging, cleaning, loan rules, content licences) are not in this evidence.
  • 63 of 131 comments are forum posts, mostly Mumsnet in the UK, while prices are in US dollars. Counts by country were not tested.
  • Only three US patents were opened. This is not a patent search.
  • No named market-size report was read. Revenue figures are company numbers as press reported them.
Why the numbers differ from tab to tabPain share is cut three ways in this brief, so the same topic can show different figures.
  • By stage of the job map, for example Prepare at 0.70 over 10 comments and Monitor at 0.93 over 15.
  • By theme, for example app, Wi-Fi and setup friction at 0.77 over 13 comments.
  • By territory, which groups the job map steps, for example Setup and upkeep at 0.84 over 25 comments covering three steps.
  • Small groups swing a lot. Treat any figure on fewer than 15 comments as a pointer, not a rate.
What a full engagement would addThis sample runs on public sources in a few hours. A real engagement adds more.
  • Several hundred more comments per source group, including Amazon and Reddit, enough to test saturation.
  • Client kickoff, so territories answer the client's own questions and constraints.
  • A patent and prior-art search, price testing and conversations with real parents, designers and retailers.
  • Ideation sessions that start from the concept cards.
  • Timing, team and price are set at scoping and are not part of this sample.
Insight
